title: Read analyse and respond to a variety of texts

lessons.title: Reading strategies for workplace texts
lessons.html:
Different texts, different ways of reading

On a farm or in a processing plant you read many kinds of text: product labels, standard operating procedures (SOPs), safety data sheets, employment contracts, circulars from the Department of Agriculture, market reports, emails, WhatsApp messages, newspaper articles and graphs of production figures. A good reader chooses the right strategy for the text and the purpose.

Three reading strategies

StrategyWhat you doExample
SkimmingRead quickly for the general idea: headings, first sentences, picturesDeciding whether a magazine article on drip irrigation is worth reading
ScanningSearch for one specific piece of informationFinding the re-entry period or PPE section on a chemical label
Intensive readingRead slowly and carefully, every word, often more than onceReading a contract, a new SOP or the first-aid section of a label

Before you read

  • Ask: why am I reading this, and what do I need from it?
  • Look at the title, headings, date and author or source.
  • Think about what you already know about the topic.

While you read

  • Underline or note key words and instructions.
  • Work out unfamiliar words from the context, or look them up. Technical terms such as ‘withholding period’, ‘germination capacity’ or ‘critical control point’ have exact meanings; do not guess.
  • Notice signal words: ‘however’ introduces a contrast, ‘therefore’ a result, ‘must’ an obligation, ‘may’ a choice.
  • Stop and check your understanding at the end of each section.

Reading instructions safely

For chemical labels, machine manuals and SOPs, read the whole instruction before starting work. Pay special attention to warnings, cautions, numbered steps and words like ‘never’ and ‘only’. If something is unclear, ask your supervisor before acting. Misreading a mixing rate or a withdrawal period can harm people, animals, crops or a whole export consignment.

Reading in a second language

Many workers read English as an additional language. Read slowly, use a dictionary or a colleague to check difficult terms, and ask for important documents to be explained in your home language if needed. Asking is a sign of a responsible worker.

lessons.title: Analysing texts: purpose, structure, language and visuals
lessons.html:
Looking beneath the surface

To analyse a text is to work out how and why it was written, not only what it says.

Purpose and audience

Texts may inform (a market report), instruct (an SOP), persuade (an advertisement for a fertiliser), regulate (a regulation or contract) or entertain (a story). Ask who the text was written for: a farmer, a consumer, a government official? The purpose and audience explain the choices the writer made.

Structure

  • Reports have headings, findings and recommendations.
  • Instructions have numbered steps in order.
  • Arguments state a position, give reasons and evidence, and conclude.
  • News articles put the most important facts first.

Language choices

  • Fact and opinion: facts can be checked; opinions show what someone thinks. ‘The dam is at 35% of capacity’ is a fact; ‘The drought is the worst disaster ever’ is opinion.
  • Connotation: words carry feelings. ‘Cheap’ and ‘affordable’ mean similar things but feel different.
  • Bias: a one-sided text leaves out other views or facts. Check who wrote it and who benefits.
  • Stereotypes: watch for language that unfairly labels groups of people by race, gender, age or origin.
  • Register: formal language suits a letter to the bank; informal language suits a message to a colleague.

Visual texts

Graphs, tables, maps, posters, safety signs and advertisements are also texts. When reading a graph, check the title, the axis labels and units, the scale and the source. A bar graph whose vertical axis starts at 90 instead of 0 can make a small difference look huge. In advertisements, ask what the picture suggests: a smiling farmer in a green field suggests success, but it is not evidence that the product works.

Example analysis

A seed company brochure says: ‘Farmers love our new cultivar – record yields everywhere!’ Purpose: persuade. Audience: farmers. Language: emotional, exaggerated (‘everywhere’, ‘record’). Evidence: none given. A critical reader asks for trial data from their own region and season before deciding.

lessons.title: Responding to texts
lessons.html:
Turning reading into action

Reading is only useful if you can respond: summarise it, explain it to others, use it in your work, or answer it.

Summarising

  1. Read the text and identify the main idea of each paragraph or section.
  2. Leave out examples, repetition and minor details.
  3. Write the main points in your own words, in a logical order.
  4. Check that the summary is accurate and fair to the original.

For example, a supervisor may summarise a new two-page hygiene SOP into five points for the morning toolbox talk.

Giving a critical response

A critical response gives your considered view, supported by reasons. Use this pattern:

  • State what the text says (briefly).
  • Say what you agree with and why.
  • Say what you question, with evidence: ‘The article says water use will drop by half, but it gives no figures for our soil type.’
  • Suggest what further information is needed.

Using information from several texts

Managers often compare texts: three quotations for a pump, two market reports, or advice from a vet and from a feed company. Make a simple table comparing them on the same points, such as price, delivery time and guarantee. Note where sources agree and where they differ, and which source is more reliable.

Responding in writing or speech

You may respond with a reply email, a report to management, a completed form, or a short talk to your team. Match your response to its purpose and audience, and refer back to the text accurately, for example by quoting the clause number of a contract or the page of a manual.

Reading for personal growth

Reading farming magazines, labour law guides, financial articles and stories improves vocabulary and confidence. Set a small goal, such as one article a week, and discuss it with a colleague.

Key points

  • Skim for the general idea, scan for specific facts and read intensively for instructions and contracts.
  • Analyse purpose, audience, structure and language choices.
  • Separate fact from opinion and look for bias and missing information.
  • Check titles, axes, scales and sources when reading graphs.
  • Respond with accurate summaries and reasoned, evidence-based views.
